newsitem.title: KENYA: Uganda declares state coffee reforms a success.
newsitem.headline: Uganda declares state coffee reforms a success.

text.p: Ugandan coffee authorities said on Tuesday the good 1995/96 crop year illustrated the success of the liberalisation policy the government launched in 1990.
In the final quarterly report for 1995/96 (October/September), the Uganda Coffee Development Authority (UCDA) said the year saw a record export volume of 4.15 million 60 kg (132.3 lb) bags.

"This is no mean achievement compared with an annual average of 2.4 million 60 kg bags before and immediately after liberalisation," UCDA said. "This clearly demonstrates the effectiveness of government liberalisation policy on coffee."
For the 1996/97 year, coffee procurement was estimated at 3.75 million bags, with exports at 3.6 million bags.
UCDA also attributed the 1995/96 gains to good weather, especially timely and adequate rainfall that prevailed in most growing areas making it possible to harvest the crop year round.
It listed other reasons for improvement as:
-- The coming into full production of the clonal (robusta) variety planted three to four years ago.
-- The 1994 price incentive coupled with the availability of crop finance, which led to good husbandry at the farm level.

-- An inverse price structure and volatility in international prices that made stock-holding risky. Players at every level of the marketing chain held stocks low for fear of incurring huge losses in the event of a sudden collapse in global prices.
-- Improvements in the transportation system, allowing exporters to use any mode of transport to ports, and a reduction in the time government agencies take to process export documents.

UCDA said export earnings during the year fell in real terms by 10.1 percent to $388.9 million from $432 million in 1994/95. It said the unit value of exports declined to an annual average of $1.56 per kg (2.2 lb), down from $2.58 realised in 1994/95.

UCDA blamed the declines in average realised unit value and overall earnings on a lack of effective demand from roasters who, throughout the year, continued with a just-in buying strategy, which was adopted in 1994 after the frost in Brazil.
It said the strategy was given further support by improved transportation systems in producing countries.

It said other reasons for a decline in prices included the possibility of a steady and adequate supply in 1996/97 after the news that Brazil's production is back to normal and reports of increased production from other countries.
"World coffee supply is estimated to reach 74 million bags and consumption in importing countries is projected at 72 million bags, making a surplus of 2.0 million bags," UCDA said.

"The surplus supply situation coupled with traders' dismissal of Association of Coffee Producing Countries' ability to have an effective implementation of the second export limitation plan, gave confidence to the market," UCDA said.

"The bearish fundamental reports and continued producer selling prompted the investment funds to liquidate long positions," UCDA added in summarising why it earned less from more coffee exported in 1995/96.
